The other side

Where the alternatives are stronger

These are real trade-offs, not softened ones. If any of them is a blocker for you, one of the other tools is the better choice — and you should find that out now rather than after a migration.

No native mobile applications

Bitwarden, Vaultwarden and Passbolt ship mobile clients; Teampass does not. If your team needs credentials on phones, that is a real gap and you should weigh it seriously.

The browser extension is a paid add-on

Bitwarden and Passbolt include theirs at no cost. Ours is what funds the project, and the server stays fully usable without it — but it is a difference worth knowing before you compare price tags.

A smaller ecosystem

Bitwarden has a large company, formal audits and a broad integration ecosystem behind it. Teampass is a long-lived project with a small core team. Choose accordingly.

The case for Teampass

Three reasons teams pick it anyway

Governance is not an upsell

Recertification campaigns, evidence export, classification and rotation tracking ship in the free server. Elsewhere the equivalent features — where they exist at all — sit behind an enterprise tier.

A real folder and role model

A tree of folders with roles and per-user overrides, rather than flat collections. It maps onto how organisations actually delegate access — per client, per environment, per team.

A stack most teams already run

PHP and MySQL. No .NET, no container orchestration, no separate identity service. If you host a web application today, you can host this.

How to use this page. Do not choose a password manager from a comparison table — including this one. Install the two you are weighing, model your real folder structure in each, and try an offboarding. The differences that matter show up in fifteen minutes of that, and never in a feature grid.

Try it against your own use case.

Free, self-hosted, and uninstallable in one command if it is not for you.
